name: Soak-stain
summary: Thin paint is poured on raw, unprimed canvas that lies on the floor; the cloth drinks the colour and the colour and the weave become one.
how: Thin oil with turpentine, or acrylic with water, until it flows like ink.
Lay the canvas flat and unprimed on the floor; pour in pools and guide the paint with a sponge or a tilt of the cloth.
Leave 30% to 60% of the cloth bare so that the raw colour is part of the picture.
Work at a size of 2 metres or more so that the field is wider than the viewer's sight.

origin.note: Helen Frankenthaler pours thinned oil on raw canvas in Mountains and Sea.

adoptions.via: Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland visit the studio of Frankenthaler and take up the stain method; Louis turns it into his Veils from 1954.
Noland moves from oil to thinned acrylic, which stains the cloth with no halo; Louis stains with thinned Magna acrylic from the first Veils in 1954.
